outcome: Since 26 January 2024 I found no event that moves the bound on the maximum number of givens in a 9×9 minimal sudoku puzzle. The largest minimal puzzle on record is still a 40-given example whose source, date and grid I could not trace, and the one in-window item (Eppstein and Zhang, arXiv:2607.05728, 7 July 2026) studies a different quantity and gives no 9×9 maximum.
problem_asks: Read from the statement alone. (1) 'Sudoku': the bullet does not state a grid size; I took the standard 9×9 puzzle as the default and treated n²×n² generalisations as analogues. (2) 'Minimal puzzle': a puzzle with a unique solution from which no given can be removed without creating a second solution (Wikipedia: 'A minimal puzzle is a proper puzzle from which no clue can be removed without introducing additional solutions'). (3) 'Maximum number of givens for a minimal puzzle': the largest value, over all such 9×9 puzzles, of the number of givens. That splits into (a) the value itself; (b) a witness puzzle attaining it, which is a lower bound; (c) a proof that no minimal puzzle has more givens, which is an upper bound. A bound that is not tight leaves the question open.

events.what_happened: A forum user, 'ravel', on the dailysudoku.com forum, announced a minimal 9×9 puzzle with 38 givens, described in the thread as the first minimal puzzle with 38 clues. The thread puts publication in July 2007. Steve R congratulated ravel on 4 Aug 2007. On 5 Aug 2007 Asellus asked whether 39 or 40 givens had been found, and Steve R replied '38 is the highest yet found', adding that ravel suspected a 39 existed and was still searching. This is a forum claim only, with no paper.
events.delivers: A minimal 9×9 puzzle with 38 givens, if the forum poster's minimality claim is right. That gives a lower bound of 38 on the maximum. It establishes nothing about an upper bound.
events.remains: Everything above 38. It does not say whether any minimal puzzle has more than 38 givens.
events.directly_checkable: The 38-given grid is in the forum thread. A solver could test uniqueness and minimality, but I did not extract the grid from the page.
events.doubts: Single forum claim with no independent check. Forum replies discussed how hard the puzzle was to solve (one reply reported solving it in 8 steps, per a search snippet), not whether it is minimal. No named person is recorded as having checked minimality. The 'published 17 July' date comes from a search snippet, not from the thread text I read.
events.direction: A lower-bound example. It cuts toward large minimal puzzles existing and bears on no upper bound.
events.object: A 9×9 sudoku with 38 givens and a unique solution, claimed minimal (no given can be removed without creating a second solution). The grid is explicit in the thread but was not reproduced in my fetched summary.

events.what_happened: Lars Peters Endresen and Håvard Graff are credited, in chapter 13 ('The World's First Sudoku Thirty-Niner') of Stokes and Blair-Chappell, 'Parallel Programming with Intel Parallel Studio XE' (Wiley), with building 'what may be the world's first Sudoku puzzle that has 39 clues', using a SIMD and multicore search. I could not read the chapter beyond its opening pages (the O'Reilly page returned 403). A search summary of a publisher listing gives 2012 as the book's date, which I did not open.
events.delivers: A 9×9 puzzle with 39 givens, as described. If it is minimal, it gives a lower bound of 39 on the maximum. Neither minimality nor uniqueness is stated in any text I could read.
events.remains: Everything above 39. Whether the puzzle is minimal is unknown from the sources I read.
events.time_since_posted: about 14 years, if the year is 2012
events.directly_checkable: The 39-clue grid would be checkable by a solver if the chapter or companion code gives it. I did not obtain it.
events.doubts: Minimality is not stated. The 'may be the world's first' hedge is the authors' own. The only description I could read is a search-snippet summary, so the claim rests on a book chapter I did not read in full.
events.direction: A lower-bound example if the puzzle is minimal. Otherwise it bears on no bound.
events.object: A 39-clue 9×9 sudoku puzzle, described as found with a SIMD and multicore search. The grid is not in any source I could read.

events.what_happened: McGuire, Tugemann and Civario, 'There is no 16-Clue Sudoku: Solving the Sudoku Minimum Number of Clues Problem', arXiv:1201.0749. v1 was submitted 1 Jan 2012 and v2 on 1 Sep 2013. Wikipedia cites it as Experimental Mathematics 23(2), 2014. An exhaustive computer search, using a new hitting-set enumeration, shows that no 9×9 sudoku with 16 givens has a unique solution, so the minimum is 17. This concerns the global minimum, not the maximum over minimal puzzles.
events.revisions: v2 1 Sep 2013 (arXiv). Journal version Experimental Mathematics 2014, cited by Wikipedia; journal page not opened.
events.delivers: The least number of givens of any 9×9 puzzle with a unique solution is 17. It establishes nothing about the largest minimal puzzle.

checked_by.qualification: Journal referees for a computational combinatorics paper
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted the paper for publication, according to the Wikipedia citation. I did not open the journal page.

events.directly_checkable: Not by hand. The result is an exhaustive computer search. I found no formal (Lean, Coq or Rocq) check of it.
events.doubts: The result is computer-assisted and I did not inspect its code. One undated blog snippet said the proof's details were still being checked. None of this bears on the maximum.
events.direction: Confirms the minimum of 17. Does not touch the maximum.

ai.disclosed_cost: A third-party search snippet reports about 7 million CPU hours. I did not confirm this in the abstract page I read.

events.what_happened: Tjusila, Besançon, Turner and Koch, 'How Many Clues To Give? A Bilevel Formulation For The Minimum Sudoku Clue Problem', arXiv:2305.01697 (v1 2 May 2023). Operations Research Letters 54 (2024) 107105, per a search summary that I did not open. For a given completed grid, the problem asks for the fewest givens of a unique puzzle with that solution. The authors use a binary bilevel LP and report solving 95% of 50 9×9 instances to optimality.
events.revisions: Journal publication 2024 (Operations Research Letters), per a search summary. Not opened.
events.delivers: Computed per-grid minima for 50 9×9 grids. That is a different quantity (the least number of givens for one grid), not the maximum over minimal puzzles, so it bounds nothing here.

checked_by.qualification: Journal referees for an optimisation paper
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted the paper, per a search-summary citation (DOI 10.1016/j.orl.2024.107105). Not opened.

events.directly_checkable: Not applicable. The results are computational tables for 50 grids.
events.doubts: None specific to the maximum question. The paper is about the per-grid minimum only, so its findings do not transfer.
events.direction: Does not cut either way on the maximum. It is a neighbouring question.

events.what_happened: David Eppstein and Xinyu (Cindy) Zhang, 'Sudoku Grids That Require Many Clues', arXiv:2607.05728 (v1, 7 July 2026). For a filled grid, the paper asks for the fewest givens that make its solution unique, and then looks for grids that maximise that number. Its results are: (i) 9×9 grids that need 18 givens, built by packing nine order-3 Latin squares (each needs two givens) into the grid; (ii) a 16×16 grid that needs 80 givens, built by packing 16 copies of a 4×4 Latin square that needs 5 givens, with the 4×4 fact from 'case analysis'; (iii) Theorem 2: all but a 1/2^(n^4) fraction of filled n²×n² grids need at least n^4 − O(n^4/log n) givens. Section 3 also says that each filled grid has at least one minimal clue set, and that 'the same fraction of minimal clue sets require the same number of clues'. The paper does not define 'minimal clue set' and does not state a maximum.
events.revisions: v1 only (arXiv listing, 7 Jul 2026). No later version found.
events.delivers: Restricted to what it says. (a) 9×9: some grids need 18 givens, a lower bound on the fewest givens for those grids. That does not bear on the largest minimal puzzle, since 18 is well below 40. (b) 16×16: one grid whose every unique-solution puzzle has at least 80 givens. My inference, not the paper's statement: since every grid has at least one minimal puzzle, some 16×16 minimal puzzle has at least 80 givens. (c) Asymptotic, for large n: most n²×n² grids need n^4 − O(n^4/log n) givens. Read literally, the Section 3 remark implies large minimal puzzles exist for large n. That is an inference from a terse counting argument, not a stated theorem about maxima. No concrete 9×9 value follows.
events.remains: For 9×9, the maximum number of givens of a minimal puzzle is left unbounded in both directions: no upper bound, and no minimal puzzle beyond the 18-given lower bound. For other n, only the asymptotic claim, with no exact maximum. The 40-given record is not addressed.
events.time_since_posted: about 3 months (posted 7 Jul 2026; record compiled 13 Oct 2026)
events.directly_checkable: The 9×9 construction (nine order-3 Latin squares packed into the grid, each needing two givens) can be checked by hand from the paper's description. The 16×16 claim rests on a 4×4 Latin square needing 5 givens, which is a finite check a computer can run quickly. I did not run either check.
events.doubts: (i) One arXiv version, about three months old, with no independent reading found. (ii) The 16×16 80-given figure relies on a case analysis I could not inspect. (iii) 'Minimal clue set' is used but never defined, and the Section 3 remark is a counting argument that I read through a summarising tool, not line by line. Any reading of it as a maximum bound is my inference. (iv) The venue is 'to appear' at the Japan conference on discrete and computational geometry, graphs and games; sources disagree on the edition (26th or 28th). The co-author's own blog digest (reposted at bubbles.town) is not an independent reading, and the Emergent Mind page is an automated summary I saw only in a search snippet.
events.direction: Cuts neither way on the 9×9 maximum. It is about the fewest givens for a given grid, a different quantity. It gives an 18-given lower bound for some 9×9 grids and an 80-given grid for 16×16 that bounds that size's minimal puzzles from below. For the bullet's 9×9 question it moves no bound.
events.object: No object for the 9×9 maximum. The objects are filled grids, not minimal puzzles. (1) 9×9 grids made by packing nine order-3 Latin squares into a sudoku grid; each Latin square needs two givens, so every unique-solution puzzle for the grid has at least 18 givens. Explicit construction. (2) A 16×16 grid made by packing 16 copies of a 4×4 Latin square that needs 5 givens, so every unique-solution puzzle for it has at least 80 givens. Explicit construction, with the 4×4 fact from case analysis.

events.what_happened: A sentence saying 'the largest minimal puzzle found so far has 40 clues in the 81 cells'. Search snippets attribute it to Wikipedia's 'Mathematics of Sudoku' article. Two fetches of the current article (rendered page, and raw wikitext under the lower-case title) found no such sentence and no figure for the largest minimal puzzle. They did find 'Different minimal sudokus can have a different number of clues'. The article history shows edits on 25 June 2026 ('refactor; remove an unsourced section', −4,721 bytes) and 4 October 2026 ('rm claims in lead that are neither sourced nor elaborated in the body', −213 bytes). The history shows summaries and byte counts only, so I cannot tell whether either removed this sentence. No source gives a discoverer, date or grid for a 40-given minimal puzzle.
events.revisions: Edits on 25 Jun 2026 and 4 Oct 2026 are listed in the article history. Whether either removed this sentence is unknown. The article as it stood on 26 Jan 2024 could not be retrieved; the Internet Archive snapshot was refused.
events.delivers: If accurate, a minimal 9×9 puzzle with 40 givens, which is a lower bound of 40 on the maximum. It sets no upper bound. The wording 'found so far' says as much.
events.remains: The upper bound and the exact maximum.
events.directly_checkable: The puzzle is not reproduced in any source I could read, so the record cannot be checked as it stands. A solver run would need the grid and clue set.
events.doubts: The sentence is unsourced in what I could read. It is missing from the current article text, which I fetched twice. It cannot be dated. Its predecessors (38 in 2007, and 39 credited to Endresen and Graff) do not establish it. The SudokuWiki claim below, that 39 is the most clues a minimal puzzle can have, directly contradicts it.
events.direction: If accurate, a lower-bound example of 40 for the maximum. It leans toward large minimal puzzles existing and says nothing about an upper bound.
events.object: Per the snippet, a minimal 9×9 puzzle with 40 givens in the 81 cells. No grid, clue set or discoverer appears in any source I could read.

events.what_happened: A search summary attributes to SudokuWiki's 'Sudoku Creation and Grading' paper (by Andrew Stuart) the statement that '39 numbers is the most number of clues that a minimal puzzle can have'. I could not verify it. The fetch returned the PDF as compressed binary, and the readable part I could extract says nothing about clue counts. I did not open the copy the fetch saved to disk, because it sits outside the project directory.
events.delivers: If the claim is accurate, an upper bound of 39 on minimal puzzles. That would be a result on the question itself, and it would contradict the 40-given figure. It is not established.
events.remains: Everything, if the claim is unverified.
events.directly_checkable: Not applicable until the document text is read.
events.doubts: Unverified. It comes from a search summary only and conflicts with the 40-given figure in the Wikipedia event. One of the two is wrong, or they use 'minimal' differently. The judging pass needs the document text.
events.direction: If accurate, it cuts against the 40-given example by asserting an upper bound of 39.

disputes.summary: The largest minimal sudoku is 40 givens according to the Wikipedia sentence in search snippets. A SudokuWiki paper, as reported in a search summary, says 39 is the most clues a minimal puzzle can have. Both cannot hold in the sense stated. The 40 sentence is absent from the current Wikipedia text I fetched, and the SudokuWiki text I could read does not mention clue counts.

summary: I ran 49 web searches and a few dozen page fetches. No event since 26 January 2024 moves the 9×9 maximum. The only in-window item is Eppstein and Zhang, arXiv:2607.05728 (7 July 2026, one version). I read it from the arXiv HTML rendering, since the PDF body was not readable. It asks a different quantity (the fewest givens that make a given grid's solution unique) and gives 9×9 grids needing 18 givens, a 16×16 grid needing 80 (by case analysis and packing), and an asymptotic theorem for n²×n² grids. Section 3 also says each filled grid has at least one minimal clue set, and that the same fraction of minimal clue sets need the same number of givens. Read literally that implies large minimal puzzles exist for large n, but it is stated only asymptotically, 'minimal clue set' is never defined, and no maximum or 9×9 value is given. The 18-given lower bound is far below 40, so the 9×9 question is untouched. The 16×16 inference (at least 80 givens for some minimal puzzle) is mine, from the paper's own claim. The 40-given record is the central unresolved item. Search snippets attribute to Wikipedia the sentence 'the largest minimal puzzle found so far has 40 clues in the 81 cells'. Two fetches of the current article (rendered, and raw wikitext) do not contain that sentence, and the history shows two later removal edits (25 June 2026 and 4 October 2026) whose text I could not see. I could not retrieve the 25 January 2024 revision, so I cannot say whether the sentence was in the frozen article or how it was sourced. Predecessor milestones are a 38-given puzzle announced on a forum in July 2007 ('38 is the highest yet found', 5 Aug 2007) and a 39-given puzzle credited to Endresen and Graff, described in a 2012-dated book chapter whose minimality the sources I read do not state. The sharpest conflict is a SudokuWiki claim, seen only in a search summary, that 39 is the most clues a minimal puzzle can have. I could not read that PDF text, and I did not open the copy saved outside the project. If the 39 claim is right, the 40 figure is wrong; if 40 is right, the SudokuWiki claim is wrong or uses 'minimal' differently. McGuire, Tugemann and Civario (2012, arXiv:1201.0749) and Tjusila et al. (2023, arXiv:2305.01697) are recorded as discounted events: the first fixes the global minimum at 17, and the second computes per-grid minima. Neither bears on the maximum. AI: no source connects an AI system to minimal-puzzle clue counts. Searches on AlphaEvolve, AlphaProof, GPT-5, Claude, Gemini and OpenAI or DeepMind 2026 announcements (including Erdős problems) found nothing on this question. The full HTML of the 2026 preprint credits only an NSF grant. One search snippet placed a GPT-5-nano sudoku prompt in arXiv:2608.12486 (DIVE). The abstract page I opened has no sudoku content, so I could not resolve that from it. The paper is about LLM skill evolution, and any sudoku use would be a solving benchmark, not clue-count mathematics. None of the events therefore names an AI system.
competing_reading: (a) The Section 3 remark, read as a theorem, already gives the asymptotic answer for large n (most minimal clue sets have about n^4 givens), so the problem's status would be 'bounded below by n^4 − O(n^4/log n) for large n' and open for 9×9. (b) The 40-given sentence, if it was in the frozen article and correct, is an established lower bound, so the 9×9 maximum is open above 40. (c) The SudokuWiki 39 claim, if correct, would close the 9×9 question at 39 and make the 40 record false. (d) The 16×16 80-given result is an answer for a different grid size, which the bullet, read as 9×9, does not ask. Whether the bullet covers all n²×n² sudoku is a call for the judging pass.
what_would_settle_it: (1) The Wikipedia revision at or before 26 Jan 2024 (and the edit that first added the 40 sentence, with its citation); the 25 Jun and 4 Oct 2026 diffs would show whether the sentence was removed. (2) The grid and clue set of the 40-given puzzle, tested for uniqueness and minimality by a solver, plus the discoverer and date. (3) The full text of the SudokuWiki 'Sudoku Creation and Grading' paper, read for the sentence about 39. (4) The full definition of 'minimal clue set' in arXiv:2607.05728 and the exact statement of its Section 3 claim, to settle whether the maximum is implied. (5) A 9×9 upper bound, or any larger minimal puzzle, from a checked source.
